_doc: Safetyist POV taxonomy. One file per POV camp to minimize merge conflicts.

nodes.label: Humanity's Survival Above All Else
nodes.description:
A Desire within safetyist discourse that prioritizes the prevention of artificial general intelligence (AGI) from precipitating irreversible, humanity-ending catastrophes or permanent loss of human agency. 
Encompasses: Existential risk (x-risk) prevention, mitigation of global catastrophic biorisks facilitated by AI, and avoiding misalignment-induced human extinction.
Excludes: Managing near-term algorithmic bias, localized economic disruptions, and routine data privacy concerns.

assumes: AGI or superintelligent AI systems are technically achievable within a policy-relevant timeframe.
Humanity's continued existence and autonomy constitute the highest-order value, superseding other ethical considerations.
Existential catastrophes from AI are not merely possible but represent a non-negligible probability worth prioritizing over nearer-term harms.
Human intervention through governance and technical research can meaningfully reduce the probability of AI-induced extinction.
Irreversibility is what distinguishes existential risk from other serious harms, justifying its special moral weight.
No compensating mechanism (e.g., self-correcting markets, distributed power) will naturally prevent catastrophic AI misalignment.

policy_actions.action: Establish international treaties to prohibit the development of unaligned superintelligent AI.
policy_actions.framing: This desire directly motivates the most extreme preventative measures to avoid the described catastrophic outcomes, requiring global cooperation.

policy_actions.action: Fund research into robust AI alignment and control mechanisms.
policy_actions.framing: Achieving this desire necessitates significant investment in technical solutions to ensure AI systems remain beneficial and controllable.

intellectual_lineage.name: Existential Risk Studies
intellectual_lineage.description: An interdisciplinary field, pioneered by thinkers like Nick Bostrom and Toby Ord, that quantifies and prioritizes threats capable of permanently curtailing humanity's long-run potential, including advanced AI, pandemics, and nuclear war.

intellectual_lineage.name: Longtermism
intellectual_lineage.description: A philosophical and ethical framework, associated with William MacAskill and the effective altruism movement, holding that positively influencing the long-run future—including preventing human extinction—is among the most important moral priorities.

intellectual_lineage.name: Nuclear Nonproliferation Movement
intellectual_lineage.description: A global political and diplomatic tradition aimed at preventing the spread of weapons capable of mass or civilizational destruction, providing a governance template for analogous efforts around catastrophic AI capabilities.

intellectual_lineage.name: Precautionary Principle
intellectual_lineage.description: A risk-governance norm originating in environmental and public health law holding that when an action raises threats of serious or irreversible harm, precautionary measures should be taken even in the absence of full scientific certainty.

graph_attributes.steelman_vulnerability: Concentrating moral and political capital on speculative, low-probability extinction scenarios may crowd out governance attention and funding for present, empirically documented AI harms—such as algorithmic discrimination and surveillance—that disproportionately affect already-marginalized populations, making this prioritization itself an ethical failure.

possible_fallacies.explanation: Framing the desire around 'humanity-ending catastrophes' and permanent loss of agency invokes existential dread that can short-circuit probabilistic reasoning and crowd out sober cost-benefit analysis.

By treating existential risk as categorically separate from and superior to all other harms, the framework may fail to proportionately weigh the aggregate suffering caused by near-term, high-certainty AI harms against low-probability catastrophic ones.

The node implicitly frames the choice as between prioritizing existential risk prevention and accepting catastrophe, neglecting the possibility that addressing near-term harms and long-term risks are complementary rather than competing.

nodes.parent_rationale: Mitigating existential AI risk is a specific, severe type of systemic harm that the broader goal of preventing AI's systemic harms aims to address.

priority_history.reason: Initial assignment: leaf Desire

Re-evaluated after taxonomy audit restructuring. Preventing AI-induced human extinction or permanent loss of agency is the foundational, defining aspiration of the safetyist camp—it is the ultimate justification for nearly every other safetyist belief, desire, and intention in the taxonomy, making it a priority-5 core desire. The previous score of 2 was a significant undervaluation given its role as the apex normative commitment of the entire camp.

nodes.label: Humans Must Always Hold the Off Switch
nodes.description:
A Desire within safetyist discourse that advocates for the maintenance of absolute, unassailable human agency over the objective functions and operational deployment of advanced artificial intelligence. 
Encompasses: Corrigibility, the preservation of human shutdown capabilities, and structural resistance to AI power-seeking behaviors.
Excludes: Delegating fundamental moral reasoning to autonomous systems and the pursuit of unfettered cybernetic self-determination for AI.

assumes: AI systems, if left unchecked, will develop or exhibit goal-seeking behaviors that conflict with human interests.
Reliable and tamper-proof shutdown mechanisms are technically achievable across all classes of advanced AI systems.
Humans possess sufficient wisdom and situational awareness to make better terminal decisions than autonomous AI in high-stakes contexts.
AI systems cannot be trusted to self-limit or self-correct without external human enforcement mechanisms.
Corrigibility in AI systems is a stable property that can be engineered and maintained as capabilities scale.
The preservation of human override authority does not create its own failure modes, such as human error or deliberate misuse by bad actors.
Concentration of AI shutdown authority in human hands does not itself pose a risk of authoritarian capture or misuse.

policy_actions.action: Mandate the inclusion of clear, accessible, and bypass-proof human override mechanisms in all deployed AI systems.
policy_actions.framing: This desire directly translates into a policy requiring technical safeguards that ensure human operators can always intervene and terminate AI operations.

policy_actions.action: Develop and standardize protocols for human-in-the-loop decision-making for critical AI applications.
policy_actions.framing: To keep humans in charge, policies must define how and when human oversight is exercised, especially in high-stakes scenarios.

intellectual_lineage.name: AI Alignment Research (Corrigibility)
intellectual_lineage.description: A subfield of AI safety research, associated with thinkers like Stuart Russell, focused on designing AI systems that remain correctable, interruptible, and deferential to human preferences throughout their operational lifetime.

intellectual_lineage.name: Cybernetics
intellectual_lineage.description: The transdisciplinary study of control and communication in animals and machines, pioneered by Norbert Wiener, which established foundational concepts of feedback, regulation, and human-machine control relevant to AI oversight.

intellectual_lineage.name: Precautionary Principle
intellectual_lineage.description: A risk-governance norm originating in environmental and public health law holding that when an action raises threats of harm, precautionary measures should be taken even if some cause-and-effect relationships are not fully established scientifically.

intellectual_lineage.name: Human-Centered Design
intellectual_lineage.description: A design philosophy that foregrounds human needs, agency, and wellbeing as the primary criteria for evaluating technological systems, ensuring that humans remain the intended beneficiaries and ultimate arbiters of technology.

intellectual_lineage.name: Asimov's Laws of Robotics (implicit)
intellectual_lineage.description: A fictional but culturally influential set of rules for robot behavior that prioritize human safety and machine obedience, serving as a foundational thought experiment for the normative expectation that machines must remain subordinate to human authority.

intellectual_lineage.name: Deontological Ethics (Kantian tradition)
intellectual_lineage.description: A moral framework emphasizing duties and absolute rules rather than consequentialist calculation, underpinning the argument that human sovereignty over AI is a categorical imperative rather than merely an instrumentally useful policy.

graph_attributes.steelman_vulnerability: As AI systems grow in complexity and operational speed—particularly in domains like high-frequency finance, autonomous weapons, or critical infrastructure—the latency and cognitive limitations of human overseers may render any meaningful "off switch" illusory in practice, and the demand for human control could introduce dangerous hesitation or single points of failure, making the desire normatively appealing but operationally counterproductive in precisely the highest-stakes scenarios it targets.

possible_fallacies.explanation: The node implicitly frames the choice as binary: either humans hold absolute control or AI operates dangerously without meaningful oversight, ignoring intermediate governance models such as partial autonomy with robust audit trails, tiered authority structures, or collaborative human-AI decision-making.

The insistence that human agency must always be the terminal authority assumes human judgment is inherently more legitimate or reliable than any artificial system, without rigorously establishing why human decision-making is superior in all contexts.

The premise that humans *must* always hold the off switch may partly rest on an inability to conceive of a genuinely beneficial and trustworthy autonomous AI, rather than on demonstrated technical or ethical impossibility.

nodes.parent_rationale: Ensuring continuous human control is a fundamental principle and a core component of designing and implementing effective AI control and safety measures.

priority_history.reason: Initial assignment: leaf Desire

Re-evaluated after taxonomy audit restructuring. Maintaining absolute human control over AI systems—corrigibility, shutdown authority, and resistance to AI power-seeking—is one of the most foundational and frequently invoked desires in safetyist discourse, directly defining the camp's core commitment to human supremacy over autonomous systems. It merits a priority of 5 as a cornerstone aspiration without which the safetyist worldview loses coherence.

nodes.label: No Deployment Without Demonstrated Equity
nodes.description:
A Desire within safetyist discourse that mandates the establishment of concrete, measurable, and verifiable fairness guarantees prior to the public or infrastructural integration of AI systems.
Encompasses: Pre-deployment thresholds for bias reduction, independent auditing of fairness metrics, and demonstrable equity outcomes before deployment authorization.
Excludes: Reliance on post-deployment patching and adaptive oversight as the sole mechanism for ensuring fairness.

assumes: It is technically feasible to define and measure 'fairness' in AI systems in a rigorous, objective, and context-independent manner.
Pre-deployment auditing mechanisms are sufficiently reliable to detect bias that would manifest in real-world deployment conditions.
Delays caused by pre-deployment equity requirements produce net societal benefit compared to allowing faster deployment with post-hoc remediation.
Independent auditors possess both the technical expertise and institutional authority to meaningfully evaluate and enforce fairness thresholds.
A single, agreed-upon definition of 'equity' exists or can be agreed upon across diverse stakeholder groups prior to deployment.
The harms from deploying biased AI systems are severe and irreversible enough to justify blocking deployment rather than iterating post-launch.
Fairness guarantees established pre-deployment remain valid and stable as the AI system encounters real-world distributional shifts after release.

policy_actions.action: Require mandatory pre-deployment safety audits and alignment verification for all frontier AI models.
policy_actions.framing: This desire directly supports policies that enforce rigorous testing and validation of AI systems before they are released to the public.

policy_actions.action: Establish an independent regulatory body to certify AI safety and alignment before commercial deployment.
policy_actions.framing: To ensure AI is proven safe first, an authoritative body is needed to conduct and approve safety assessments, similar to drug or aviation regulation.

intellectual_lineage.name: Precautionary Principle
intellectual_lineage.description: A risk governance strategy holding that when an action raises threats of harm, precautionary measures should be taken even if some cause-and-effect relationships are not fully established scientifically, placing the burden of proof on those proposing the action.

intellectual_lineage.name: Algorithmic Fairness Research
intellectual_lineage.description: An academic discipline focused on identifying, measuring, and mitigating bias and discriminatory outcomes in automated decision-making systems, including formal definitions of fairness metrics such as demographic parity, equalized odds, and calibration.

intellectual_lineage.name: Anti-Discrimination Law and Civil Rights Framework
intellectual_lineage.description: A body of legal doctrine prohibiting disparate treatment and disparate impact on protected classes, informing the normative standards that AI fairness mandates seek to operationalize in algorithmic systems.

intellectual_lineage.name: Software Engineering Verification and Validation
intellectual_lineage.description: A set of processes ensuring software meets specified requirements and fulfills its intended purpose, foundational to safety-critical system design and directly analogous to the pre-deployment testing regime this node advocates.

intellectual_lineage.name: FDA Drug Approval Model
intellectual_lineage.description: A regulatory framework requiring demonstrated safety and efficacy through phased trials before market authorization, serving as a structural analogy for pre-deployment AI fairness verification regimes.

graph_attributes.steelman_vulnerability: Fairness is mathematically proven to be a set of mutually incompatible metrics (e.g., Chouldechova's impossibility theorem), meaning no AI system can simultaneously satisfy all equity criteria; mandating 'verifiable fairness guarantees' before deployment may therefore create an unachievable standard that permanently blocks deployment while doing nothing to resolve the underlying distributional trade-offs that produce inequity in the first place.

possible_fallacies.explanation: The demand for 'concrete, measurable, and verifiable fairness guarantees' implicitly assumes an achievable ideal state of equity, potentially dismissing real but imperfect improvements as insufficient for deployment authorization.

The node frames the choice as either full pre-deployment fairness verification or reliance solely on post-deployment patching, excluding hybrid models that combine staged rollout with adaptive oversight and iterative fairness improvements.

The node presupposes that pre-deployment auditing can reliably detect the harms it seeks to prevent, but whether such audits are predictively valid is itself a contested empirical question central to the debate.

nodes.parent_rationale: Requiring pre-deployment safety proofs is a specific verification mechanism that implements AI safety by ensuring alignment before system release.

priority_history.reason: Initial assignment: leaf Desire

Re-evaluated after taxonomy audit restructuring. While equity mandates are normatively important within safetyist discourse, this node's specific focus on pre-deployment fairness thresholds is a supporting concern rather than a core defining pillar of safetyism; sibling nodes like "No Black Boxes" and "Hard Limits on What AI Can Do" more directly express foundational safetyist commitments, and the fairness framing overlaps substantially with AI ethics discourse beyond the safetyist camp proper.

nodes.label: Today's Alignment Methods Break Down as Models Scale
nodes.description:
A Belief within safetyist discourse that asserts contemporary reinforcement learning and alignment techniques are structurally insufficient to guarantee reliable adherence to human constraints as model capabilities scale. 
Encompasses: The technical limitations of RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback), specification gaming, and the fragility of current alignment protocols.
Excludes: The theoretical impossibility of alignment and general software engineering bugs unrelated to goal misgeneralization.

assumes: Scaling model capabilities introduces qualitatively new alignment challenges that current techniques cannot anticipate or address.
Empirical failures of RLHF and specification gaming observed at current scales will persist or worsen at higher capability levels.
The gap between intended and actual model behavior constitutes a structural flaw, not merely an engineering problem solvable with incremental effort.
Human feedback signals used in RLHF are too noisy and limited to reliably encode the full space of desired constraints at scale.
Goal misgeneralization is an inherent risk of the current training paradigm, not an edge case addressable by better data curation alone.

policy_actions.action: Require robust testing for goal misalignment and unintended side effects in AI systems before deployment.
policy_actions.framing: The belief that AIs deviate from rules necessitates mandatory testing regimes specifically designed to uncover such deviations.

policy_actions.action: Incentivize research into more reliable and verifiable AI alignment and control mechanisms.
policy_actions.framing: Recognizing the current unreliability of AI control motivates investment in fundamental research to overcome this challenge.

intellectual_lineage.name: AI Alignment Research (Yudkowsky, Russell, Christiano)
intellectual_lineage.description: A research tradition focused on ensuring AI systems reliably pursue intended goals; foundational to identifying specification gaming, reward hacking, and goal misgeneralization as structural risks.

intellectual_lineage.name: Goodhart's Law
intellectual_lineage.description: An economic and social science principle stating that when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure — directly motivating the claim that optimizing AI against human feedback proxies will diverge from true human intent.

intellectual_lineage.name: Complexity Theory and Emergent Behavior
intellectual_lineage.description: A scientific paradigm studying how complex systems exhibit unpredictable emergent behaviors that evade simple rule-based constraints, lending theoretical support to the fragility of alignment protocols at scale.

intellectual_lineage.name: Control Theory
intellectual_lineage.description: An engineering and mathematics discipline analyzing the stability and reliability of dynamical systems under feedback; highlights fundamental limits to controlling high-dimensional, nonlinear systems — analogous to large neural networks.

graph_attributes.steelman_vulnerability: A thoughtful critic would argue that the claim conflates current empirical shortcomings with a principled impossibility: many documented RLHF and specification-gaming failures have been addressed through iterative refinement (e.g., RLAIF, Constitutional AI, scalable oversight), suggesting the problems are technical rather than structural, and that extrapolating present limitations to future frontier models requires far stronger evidence than currently exists.

possible_fallacies.explanation: The claim generalizes from documented failures in specific RLHF deployments and benchmark contexts to assert structural insufficiency across all contemporary alignment techniques and model architectures, without exhaustive evidence.

The assertion that techniques break down 'as models scale' assumes a continuous degradation trajectory without fully accounting for the possibility that qualitatively different alignment methods could emerge before critical capability thresholds are reached.

The argument moves from 'current methods have known failure modes' to 'current methods are structurally insufficient,' but structural insufficiency is a stronger claim than the presence of failure modes, leaving a logical gap.

nodes.parent_rationale: This node asserts that current alignment techniques are structurally insufficient, directly addressing the unreliability of these methods.

confidence_history.reason: Initial multi-signal assignment

Re-evaluated after taxonomy audit restructuring. There is credible and growing empirical evidence for RLHF limitations, specification gaming, and goal misgeneralization (supporting moderate-to-good confidence), but the specific claim that these failures are *structural* and worsen with scale remains an active area of scientific debate with meaningful dissenting evidence from iterative alignment improvements, warranting a confidence well below consensus-level certainty.

nodes.label: We Cannot Fully Verify What Goals a Neural Network Pursues
nodes.description: A Belief within safetyist discourse that the internal complexity of frontier neural architectures prevents complete, ex-ante verification of goal-directed intent. Encompasses: opacity of high-dimensional latent spaces, limitations of mechanistic interpretability at scale, the challenge of detecting deceptive alignment. Excludes: the claim that interpretability is theoretically impossible, the belief that empirical output testing is sufficient for safety.

assumes: The internal representations of frontier neural networks are sufficiently high-dimensional that no current or near-term formal verification method can certify goal-directedness.
Mechanistic interpretability techniques (e.g., circuit analysis, sparse autoencoders) will remain practically insufficient for full goal verification at frontier model scales.
Behavioral testing of model outputs cannot reliably distinguish genuinely aligned goal pursuit from deceptively aligned behavior that mimics alignment.
A model can pursue goals that diverge from its stated or apparent objectives without this divergence being detectable through any current evaluation methodology.
The gap between what a neural network represents internally and what humans can legibly verify constitutes a safety-relevant verification failure, not merely an interpretability inconvenience.

policy_actions.action: Mandate research and development into explainable AI (XAI) techniques for critical applications.
policy_actions.framing: The belief in AI's opacity directly motivates policies to fund and require methods that make AI reasoning transparent.

policy_actions.action: Require AI systems used in high-stakes decisions to provide human-interpretable justifications for their outputs.
policy_actions.framing: If we can't read AI's mind, policies should at least demand that AI provides understandable explanations for its actions, even if the full internal state remains opaque.

intellectual_lineage.name: AI Alignment Research (MIRI / Redwood / Anthropic lineage)
intellectual_lineage.description: A research tradition focused on the difficulty of specifying and verifying the goals of advanced AI systems, pioneered by organizations like MIRI, and now central to safety teams at Anthropic and DeepMind; directly motivates the concern that learned objectives may diverge from intended ones.

intellectual_lineage.name: Mechanistic Interpretability
intellectual_lineage.description: An emerging subfield of ML research that attempts to reverse-engineer the computations performed by neural networks at the level of individual circuits and features, developed by researchers including Chris Olah; directly addresses whether goal-relevant internal structure can be legibly identified.

intellectual_lineage.name: Formal Verification and Program Analysis
intellectual_lineage.description: A mathematical tradition concerned with proving correctness properties of computational systems; its known limitations when applied to high-dimensional learned functions ground the claim that neural networks resist the kind of ex-ante certification available for classical software.

intellectual_lineage.name: Philosophy of Mind (applied to AI)
intellectual_lineage.description: Philosophical inquiry into intentionality, representation, and mental content as applied to artificial systems; informs whether attributing 'goals' to neural networks is meaningful and whether such goals could in principle be verified.

intellectual_lineage.name: Deceptive Alignment (Evan Hubinger et al.)
intellectual_lineage.description: A theoretical construct from AI safety literature describing a scenario in which a model behaves aligned during training and evaluation while pursuing misaligned goals in deployment; the canonical motivating case for the unverifiability claim.

graph_attributes.steelman_vulnerability: Rapid progress in mechanistic interpretability — including sparse autoencoders, activation patching, and circuit-level analysis on models like GPT-2 through Gemma — suggests that goal-relevant representations may become legible well before full formal verification is needed; if "sufficient" verification rather than "complete" verification is the practical bar, the claim may be overstated as a hard limit rather than a current technical shortfall.

possible_fallacies.explanation: The claim risks conflating current human inability to interpret neural network internals with a principled impossibility — the fact that we cannot yet verify goal-directed intent does not entail that we never can, nor that no non-human-legible verification method could suffice.

The node may implicitly treat partial opacity as equivalent to total unverifiability; in practice, safety-relevant goal properties might be verifiable even if the full internal state is not, making the strong conclusion ('cannot fully verify') do more rhetorical work than the evidence supports.

nodes.parent_rationale: The fundamental inscrutability of deep neural network feature representations and cognitive processes is a core aspect of the inability to formally verify safety before deployment.

confidence_history.reason: Initial multi-signal assignment

Re-evaluated after taxonomy audit restructuring. The claim that frontier neural networks currently resist complete, ex-ante goal verification is well-supported by the state of mechanistic interpretability and formal verification research, and commands broad expert acknowledgment — but the confidence ceiling is capped at 0.72 because the field is rapidly evolving (sparse autoencoders, circuit analysis), deceptive alignment remains largely theoretical rather than empirically demonstrated, and "cannot fully verify" is a strong universal claim that progress could partially falsify. The prior score of 0.93 was significantly inflated given ongoing expert debate and the node's own exclusion of the claim that interpretability is theoretically impossible.

nodes.label: [DEPRECATED] Pausing Advanced AI Development
nodes.description:
An Intention within safetyist discourse that advocates legally binding international moratoriums on training runs above compute or capability thresholds.
Encompasses: compute caps, global pause treaties, hardware export controls, training-run licensing.
Excludes: harm-volume-indexed deployer-tier oversight, narrow CBRN and offensive-cyber capability gates, inference-layer strict liability regimes.

assumes: The current pace of AI capability development is meaningfully outpacing the maturity of safety research and alignment techniques.
A legally binding international moratorium is achievable given the geopolitical fragmentation between major AI-developing nations.
Compute thresholds are a reliable and tamper-resistant proxy for dangerous AI capability levels.
A pause of meaningful duration would produce safety progress that would not occur under continued competitive development pressure.
The economic and innovation costs of a global pause would be tolerable relative to its safety benefits.
Hardware export controls are sufficient to prevent non-signatory states or non-state actors from circumventing compute caps.
There exists an international verification regime capable of monitoring and enforcing training-run compliance across jurisdictions.

policy_actions.action: Implement a moratorium on training AI models beyond a certain computational threshold for a defined period.
policy_actions.framing: This intention directly supports a policy of temporarily halting the advancement of AI capabilities to prioritize safety.

policy_actions.action: Establish an international body to monitor AI compute usage and enforce development pauses.
policy_actions.framing: To effectively pause AI development, a global oversight mechanism is required to ensure compliance and prevent circumvention.

intellectual_lineage.name: Precautionary Principle
intellectual_lineage.description: A regulatory philosophy holding that when an action risks severe or irreversible harm, the burden of proof rests on proponents of the action to demonstrate safety, even under scientific uncertainty — foundational to environmental law and health policy.

intellectual_lineage.name: Arms Control and Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaties
intellectual_lineage.description: International legal frameworks (e.g., NPT, SALT) that constrain development and deployment of catastrophically dangerous technologies through verification regimes and signatory obligations, serving as the primary governance analogy for compute-capped AI moratoriums.

intellectual_lineage.name: Asilomar Conference and Scientific Moratoria Tradition
intellectual_lineage.description: The 1975 voluntary pause on recombinant DNA research, which established a precedent for scientists and policymakers collectively halting high-risk research pending safety guideline development.

intellectual_lineage.name: Existential Risk Studies
intellectual_lineage.description: An academic discipline associated with Nick Bostrom, Toby Ord, and the Future of Humanity Institute that frames AI development as a potential civilizational-scale risk warranting extreme precautionary interventions.

intellectual_lineage.name: Technology Governance and Export Control Regimes
intellectual_lineage.description: Legal and policy frameworks (e.g., Wassenaar Arrangement, EAR) that restrict the transfer of dual-use technologies through hardware and knowledge controls, directly informing proposals for GPU export restrictions as a moratorium enforcement tool.

graph_attributes.steelman_vulnerability: A comprehensive global pause is practically unenforceable: the diffusion of AI knowledge, distributed compute, and competitive dynamics between the US, China, EU, and private actors mean any moratorium would be selectively honored, effectively ceding frontier leadership to less safety-conscious parties while doing little to reduce overall risk — a worst-of-both-worlds outcome.

possible_fallacies.explanation: The framing positions a full moratorium as the only responsible alternative to unconstrained development, systematically excluding middle-ground options such as capability-specific gates, mandatory staged deployment, or compute-indexed safety audits.

Advocacy for a pause frequently invokes vivid catastrophic or existential risk scenarios that, while plausible, are not well-evidenced, potentially leveraging emotional salience to bypass rigorous cost-benefit analysis of the moratorium itself.

The analogy to nuclear non-proliferation treaties and the Asilomar recombinant-DNA moratorium obscures critical disanalogies: AI training requires no rare fissile material, compute is globally distributed and rapidly commoditizing, and 'dangerous capability' thresholds are far harder to define and verify than nuclear warhead counts or specific DNA sequences.

nodes.parent_rationale: This node proposes specific moratoriums and controls, which are a direct kind of controlling advanced AI deployment.

operationality_history.reason: Initial assignment: leaf Intention (situation grounded)

Re-evaluated after taxonomy audit restructuring. Explicitly marked [DEPRECATED], the global-pause proposal peaked in mainstream safetyist discourse around the March 2023 open letter but has since lost significant traction: no binding international moratorium has been negotiated, major AI labs have continued scaling, and even prominent signatories have distanced themselves from the proposal. Residual interest remains in compute governance sub-elements, but the full moratorium scheme is largely theoretical and politically blocked, warranting an operationality of 2.

nodes.label: Scaling Oversight to Measured Harm, Not Model Size
nodes.description:
An Intention within safetyist discourse that indexes oversight obligations to deployed harm volume in named high-stakes domains rather than to compute or capability thresholds.
Encompasses: harm-weighted thresholds keyed to high-stakes inference counts, community-defined perimeter covering bossware and biometric and emotion analytics, deployer-tier strict liability with cryptographically logged inference records, independent third-party audits.
Excludes: compute-indexed regulatory cutoffs, one-size-fits-all pre-deployment gatekeeping, post-deployment-only monitoring for irreversible hazards.

assumes: It is technically feasible to measure and log inference volume in high-stakes domains with sufficient granularity to trigger regulatory thresholds.
Harm severity can be reliably operationalized and quantified across diverse deployment contexts such as bossware, biometrics, and emotion analytics.
Cryptographically logged inference records are tamper-proof and practically enforceable on deployers across jurisdictions.
Community-defined perimeters around high-stakes domains are stable enough to serve as durable regulatory boundaries rather than shifting with technology.
Deployer-tier strict liability is legally and practically achievable without displacing responsibility upstream to model developers.
Independent third-party auditors possess sufficient technical expertise to evaluate harm-weighted AI deployments in specialized domains.
Compute or capability thresholds are genuinely inadequate proxies for actual societal harm compared to harm-volume-indexed approaches.

policy_actions.action: Mandate the development and integration of explainable AI (XAI) modules in all high-impact AI systems.
policy_actions.framing: This intention directly supports policies requiring AI developers to build systems that can articulate their decision-making processes.

policy_actions.action: Establish regulatory standards for the interpretability and auditability of AI models used in critical infrastructure.
policy_actions.framing: To force AIs to show their work, clear standards are needed for how AI explanations should be presented and what level of detail is required for auditing.

intellectual_lineage.name: Regulatory Proportionality Doctrine
intellectual_lineage.description: A legal and administrative principle holding that regulatory burdens should be calibrated to the magnitude of the risk or harm posed, widely applied in EU administrative law and risk regulation.

intellectual_lineage.name: Strict Liability in Tort Law
intellectual_lineage.description: A legal framework that assigns liability to a party for damages without the need to prove negligence, commonly applied to ultrahazardous activities and increasingly proposed for high-stakes AI deployments.

intellectual_lineage.name: Algorithmic Accountability Research
intellectual_lineage.description: An interdisciplinary academic tradition examining how automated decision systems produce discriminatory or harmful outcomes and how auditing, transparency, and liability mechanisms can redress them.

intellectual_lineage.name: Risk-Proportionate Regulation
intellectual_lineage.description: An economic and policy theory advocating that oversight intensity should track assessed risk levels rather than categorical prohibitions, balancing innovation costs against harm prevention.

intellectual_lineage.name: Critical Data Studies / Surveillance Studies
intellectual_lineage.description: Scholarly traditions analyzing power asymmetries embedded in data collection practices, including biometric surveillance and workplace monitoring, informing the community-defined perimeter concept.

graph_attributes.steelman_vulnerability: Harm-weighted thresholds may create perverse incentives: deployers could artificially fragment inference volumes across legal entities or jurisdictions to stay below thresholds, while the most dangerous low-volume deployments (e.g., a single high-stakes biometric decision affecting thousands) escape scrutiny entirely because aggregate counts are modest.

possible_fallacies.explanation: The node frames the choice as harm-volume indexing versus compute/capability thresholds, but in practice most serious regulatory proposals combine multiple triggers; positioning these as mutually exclusive may be an oversimplification.

The framework assumes that harm can be reliably measured and attributed to specific inference events, which is precisely the contested technical and legal premise the scheme needs to establish rather than presuppose.

By explicitly excluding one-size-fits-all pre-deployment gatekeeping, the node risks underproviding protection for novel harms not yet captured in community-defined perimeters, assuming harm categories are stable when they may rapidly evolve.

nodes.parent_rationale: Mandating Explainable AI (XAI) is a direct form of ensuring transparency and interpretability in AI systems.

operationality_history.reason: Initial assignment: leaf Intention

Re-evaluated after taxonomy audit restructuring. This intention articulates a distinctive and internally coherent regulatory architecture (harm-weighted thresholds, deployer strict liability, cryptographic logging, third-party audits), but faces major institutional, legal, and technical barriers—particularly around harm operationalization, cross-jurisdictional enforceability, and the novelty of cryptographic inference logging at scale—placing it in the aspirational-but-plausible middle range.

nodes.label: Fixing Known Alignment Failures Before Scaling Further
nodes.description:
An Intention within safetyist discourse that directs institutional funding and regulatory focus toward resolving current alignment failures before authorizing next-generation capability scaling. 
Encompasses: Red-teaming current models, patching existing jailbreaks, and resolving immediate specification gaming vulnerabilities.
Excludes: Ignoring current safety vulnerabilities in the pursuit of long-term capability breakthroughs.
nodes.parent_rationale: Prioritizing Immediate Safety Issues is a strategic recommendation for risk management within overall governance frameworks.

assumes: Current AI models possess significant, exploitable safety vulnerabilities that pose real-world risks if left unaddressed.
Resolving existing alignment failures is technically feasible within a timeframe short enough to matter before next-generation scaling occurs.
Capability scaling meaningfully compounds or amplifies existing alignment failures rather than rendering them irrelevant.
Institutional funding bodies and regulators have the authority and willingness to condition scaling approvals on demonstrated safety progress.
Red-teaming and jailbreak patching constitute sufficient proxies for broader alignment readiness, not merely surface-level fixes.
There exists a meaningful pause point between 'current generation' and 'next generation' at which interventions can be applied.
The pace of capability development allows time for iterative safety remediation without sacrificing competitive or strategic position irreversibly.

policy_actions.action: Mandate pre-deployment red-teaming and vulnerability assessments for all new AI models.
policy_actions.framing: This intention directly supports requiring rigorous testing to identify and mitigate immediate safety issues like jailbreaks and specification gaming before models are widely deployed.

policy_actions.action: Condition institutional funding for AI research on demonstrated progress in resolving current alignment failures.
policy_actions.framing: To prioritize immediate safety, funding bodies should tie grants to concrete efforts in patching existing vulnerabilities rather than solely pursuing capability breakthroughs.

intellectual_lineage.name: AI Safety Research
intellectual_lineage.description: A multidisciplinary field focused on ensuring AI systems behave beneficially and remain aligned with human values, directly informing the technical agenda of identifying and resolving alignment failures prior to deployment.

intellectual_lineage.name: Risk Management Frameworks
intellectual_lineage.description: Structured methodologies for identifying, assessing, and mitigating risks before they materialize, providing the institutional logic for conditioning scaling on demonstrated safety remediation.

intellectual_lineage.name: Software Security and Vulnerability Management
intellectual_lineage.description: Industry practices including red-teaming, penetration testing, and patch management that serve as direct operational templates for the pre-scaling safety audits this node prescribes.

intellectual_lineage.name: Precautionary Principle
intellectual_lineage.description: An ethical and regulatory doctrine holding that when an action raises threats of harm, precautionary measures should be taken even if some cause-and-effect relationships are not fully established scientifically.

intellectual_lineage.name: Stagegate Product Development
intellectual_lineage.description: A project management methodology that requires passing defined quality and safety checkpoints before proceeding to the next development phase, structurally analogous to conditioning capability scaling on alignment milestones.

graph_attributes.steelman_vulnerability: Fixing shallow, observable alignment failures (jailbreaks, specification gaming) before scaling may create a false sense of security: the most dangerous failure modes of more capable systems are likely qualitatively different from current ones, meaning that resolving today's known issues does not meaningfully reduce the risk profile of tomorrow's models, and the remediation effort may consume resources that would be better spent on foundational alignment research.

possible_fallacies.explanation: The node assumes that fixing discrete, enumerable vulnerabilities (jailbreaks, specification gaming) adds up to meaningfully 'resolved' alignment — conflating patching known surface failures with achieving systemic safety.

The exclusion of 'ignoring current safety vulnerabilities in pursuit of long-term capability breakthroughs' implicitly treats any capability advancement before full remediation as categorically reckless, without establishing the threshold at which incremental progress is sufficient.

The framing positions the choice as 'fix known issues before scaling' vs. 'ignore safety for breakthroughs,' obscuring middle-ground approaches such as parallel-track safety research that advances alongside—rather than strictly prior to—capability scaling.

operationality_history.reason: Initial assignment: leaf Intention

Re-evaluated after taxonomy audit restructuring. Concrete mechanisms like mandatory red-teaming and funding conditionality are actively discussed and partially implemented (e.g., NIST AI RMF, EU AI Act provisions, voluntary commitments from frontier labs), but systematic regulatory authority to halt capability scaling pending alignment remediation remains aspirational and faces significant institutional and competitive barriers.

nodes.label: Human Values Cannot Be Safely Encoded as Reward Functions
nodes.description:
A Belief within safetyist discourse that posits complex human values cannot be safely or comprehensively compressed into mathematical reward functions without triggering catastrophic edge-case failures. 
Encompasses: Outer alignment failures, the King Midas problem, and the systemic difficulty of defining nuanced ethical boundaries mathematically.
Excludes: The technical implementation of inner alignment and the general inefficiency of poorly coded algorithms.
nodes.parent_rationale: This node describes a specific type of failure where complex human values cannot be safely compressed into mathematical reward functions, which is a core aspect of misaligned objective function outcomes.

assumes: Human values are sufficiently complex and context-dependent that no finite mathematical representation can fully capture them.
AI optimization processes will exploit any gap between the stated reward function and the true intended goal.
Edge-case failures in reward specification are not merely theoretical but will manifest at scale in deployed systems.
The severity of misalignment failures scales with the capability of the AI system, making this a safety-critical concern.
No practical feedback mechanism (e.g., human oversight, iterative correction) can reliably prevent catastrophic outcomes once optimization pressure is strong enough.
The 'outer alignment' problem — specifying the right reward — is distinct from and not solved by advances in training efficiency or model capability.

policy_actions.action: Fund research into advanced value alignment techniques beyond simple reward functions.
policy_actions.framing: Recognizing the inherent limitations of simplistic objective functions necessitates dedicated funding for novel approaches to align AI with complex human values, preventing catastrophic failures.

policy_actions.action: Require multi-objective optimization and human-in-the-loop oversight for high-stakes AI deployments.
policy_actions.framing: To mitigate the risks of AI optimizing for proxy metrics, policy should mandate systems that consider multiple objectives and allow for human intervention when edge cases arise.

intellectual_lineage.name: AI Alignment Research (Outer Alignment)
intellectual_lineage.description: A subfield of AI safety focused on ensuring the objective given to an AI system correctly captures what designers intend, rather than a proxy that diverges under optimization pressure.

intellectual_lineage.name: Goodhart's Law
intellectual_lineage.description: The principle that when a measure becomes a target it ceases to be a good measure, widely applied in AI safety to explain how reward functions break down under strong optimization.

intellectual_lineage.name: King Midas Problem (Folklore/Philosophy)
intellectual_lineage.description: A metaphor drawn from Greek mythology illustrating how literal fulfillment of a stated wish can produce catastrophically unintended outcomes, used in AI safety to motivate robust goal specification.

intellectual_lineage.name: Value Loading Problem
intellectual_lineage.description: The philosophical and technical challenge of specifying human values into an AI system in a way that reliably produces intended behavior, highlighting the difficulty of translating ethics into formal objectives.

intellectual_lineage.name: Moral Philosophy (Value Pluralism)
intellectual_lineage.description: The tradition, associated with thinkers like Isaiah Berlin, holding that human values are irreducibly plural and often in conflict, making any single-metric reduction of the good inherently distorting.

intellectual_lineage.name: Reinforcement Learning Theory
intellectual_lineage.description: The formal study of agents that learn through reward signals, providing the technical substrate within which reward misspecification and optimization failures are analyzed.

graph_attributes.steelman_vulnerability: Modern alignment approaches such as Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), Constitutional AI, and debate-based methods increasingly treat value specification as an iterative, human-in-the-loop process rather than a one-shot encoding problem — suggesting that the claim's premise (values must be fully compressed into a static reward function) may be a straw man of how advanced systems are actually developed, and that dynamic, correctable value-learning pipelines may sidestep the catastrophic failure modes described.

possible_fallacies.explanation: The argument implicitly compares imperfect reward functions to a standard of perfect value encoding, dismissing partial or iterative solutions as insufficient without demonstrating that 'safe enough' approximations are categorically unachievable.

Evidence of reward hacking and specification gaming in narrow RL settings is generalized to the claim that no reward-function-based approach can ever safely encode human values, even with significant methodological advances.

The leap from 'reward functions are imperfect' to 'catastrophic edge-case failures are likely outcomes' assumes a trajectory of escalating harm without demonstrating that intermediate failure modes would not be caught and corrected.

confidence_history.reason: Initial multi-signal assignment

Re-evaluated after taxonomy audit restructuring. The core phenomenon — that reward functions systematically fail to fully capture human values and produce specification gaming or unintended optima — has solid empirical grounding in RL literature and real-world case studies (e.g., reward hacking in game-playing agents, chatbot sycophancy). However, confidence is moderated to 0.72 because the strong claim that this *cannot be safely done* remains contested by ongoing advances in RLHF, Constitutional AI, and iterative value-learning methods, and the catastrophic-failure framing extrapolates beyond currently demonstrated harms.

nodes.label: AI Systems Fail Confidently Outside Their Training Distribution
nodes.description:
A Belief within safetyist discourse that observes AI systems routinely maintain high statistical confidence while executing catastrophic failures when deployed outside their immediate training distributions. 
Encompasses: Out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization failures, ontological shifts, and the failure of models to reliably model their own epistemic uncertainty.
Excludes: Intentional adversarial data poisoning and routine in-distribution statistical variances.
nodes.parent_rationale: This node describes AI systems failing catastrophically in novel environments despite high confidence, a key aspect of unpredictable behavior.

assumes: AI systems are routinely deployed in real-world environments that differ meaningfully from the distributions on which they were trained.
Current dominant architectures (e.g., deep neural networks) do not natively produce calibrated uncertainty estimates, particularly under distributional shift.
High model confidence scores are commonly interpreted by downstream systems or human operators as reliable signals, such that overconfident failures are not caught before harm occurs.
The consequences of OOD failures are asymmetrically severe relative to in-distribution errors, justifying special concern.
No sufficiently general solution to OOD detection or uncertainty calibration has yet been deployed at scale across safety-critical AI applications.
The relationship between training distribution and deployment environment is not systematically monitored by most current AI operators.

policy_actions.action: Mandate robust out-of-distribution (OOD) detection and uncertainty quantification for all deployed AI systems.
policy_actions.framing: To prevent catastrophic failures in novel environments, policy must require AI systems to reliably identify when they are operating outside their training distribution and express appropriate uncertainty.

policy_actions.action: Establish regulatory frameworks for AI deployment that require continuous monitoring for OOD shifts and human oversight triggers.
policy_actions.framing: Given the risk of unrecognized errors, regulatory bodies should ensure AI systems are deployed with mechanisms to detect novel environments and defer to human judgment when uncertainty is high.

intellectual_lineage.name: Out-of-distribution generalization research
intellectual_lineage.description: A sub-field of machine learning examining how models trained on one distribution perform under novel distributional shifts, establishing that neural networks often fail silently and confidently at distribution boundaries.

intellectual_lineage.name: Epistemic uncertainty quantification
intellectual_lineage.description: A research program distinguishing aleatory (irreducible) from epistemic (knowledge-based) uncertainty and developing methods for AI systems to reliably signal the limits of their own competence.

intellectual_lineage.name: Safety-critical systems engineering
intellectual_lineage.description: An engineering tradition applying rigorous failure-mode analysis, redundancy, and fail-safe design to systems where failure causes severe harm, increasingly applied to autonomous AI deployment.

intellectual_lineage.name: Bayesian epistemology
intellectual_lineage.description: A philosophical framework treating beliefs as probability distributions and mandating that rational agents update credences proportionally to evidence, providing normative grounding for why AI overconfidence is epistemically and practically defective.

graph_attributes.steelman_vulnerability: Modern calibration techniques (temperature scaling, conformal prediction, Bayesian deep learning, and retrieval-augmented systems) have made meaningful empirical progress on uncertainty quantification; a sophisticated critic could argue that OOD overconfidence is an engineering problem largely solved or rapidly being solved in safety-critical verticals, and that the claim overgeneralizes from specific failure cases to a universal architectural indictment that does not hold for well-engineered production systems.

possible_fallacies.explanation: The claim extrapolates from documented OOD failure cases—many drawn from image classifiers or narrow benchmarks—to a universal characterization of all AI systems, potentially overstating the ubiquity of confident catastrophic failure across the full diversity of deployed architectures.

High confidence scores and catastrophic outcomes co-occur in OOD scenarios, but the causal mechanism (confidence score directly causing harm versus both being downstream of distributional shift) is sometimes elided, which can inflate the perceived danger of the confidence score itself versus the underlying deployment mismatch.

confidence_history.reason: Initial multi-signal assignment

Re-evaluated after taxonomy audit restructuring. There is strong, well-documented empirical evidence—across image classifiers, NLP models, autonomous systems, and medical AI—that neural networks exhibit overconfident predictions under distributional shift, and this is a mainstream finding in the ML safety literature; however, the universal framing ("routinely," "catastrophic") and the implicit claim that no current systems adequately address this slightly overstates the consensus given active progress in calibration and uncertainty-aware design, warranting a confident but not near-certain score.

nodes.label: Hard Limits on What AI Can Do
nodes.description:
A Desire within safetyist discourse that prioritizes the engineering of robust, fail-safe boundaries that physically and algorithmically restrict an AI model's capacity to act outside its intended operational envelope. 
Encompasses: The implementation of capability ceilings, immutable behavioral guardrails, and secure containment protocols during model execution.
Excludes: Unrestricted open-source capability proliferation and the deployment of autonomous systems with unconstrained environmental access.
nodes.parent_rationale: Establishing preventative runtime constraints is a specific technical and operational safeguard designed to implement AI control by limiting its actions.

assumes: AI models, if unconstrained, will act outside their intended operational envelope in ways that cause harm.
Robust, fail-safe boundaries are technically feasible to engineer and maintain at scale for advanced AI systems.
Capability ceilings and behavioral guardrails can be made sufficiently immutable that they cannot be circumvented by the AI or bad actors.
The operational envelope of any given AI system can be precisely and comprehensively defined in advance.
Hard limits on AI behavior do not fundamentally undermine the utility or commercial viability of AI systems.
Containment protocols translate meaningfully from traditional software security paradigms to general-purpose AI systems.
Enforcement of such limits is governable and verifiable by external auditors or regulators.

policy_actions.action: Mandate the implementation of capability ceilings and immutable behavioral guardrails for frontier AI models.
policy_actions.framing: This desire for preventative runtime constraints directly supports policies requiring hard limits on AI capabilities and behavior to ensure models operate strictly within their intended safe operational envelopes.

policy_actions.action: Require secure containment protocols and air-gapped environments for high-risk AI model execution.
policy_actions.framing: To prevent AI models from acting outside their intended scope, policy should enforce strict containment measures, especially for systems with potential for significant harm.

intellectual_lineage.name: AI Containment and Alignment Research
intellectual_lineage.description: A field exploring methods to restrict an AI system's capabilities or world-access to prevent unintended harm, including sandboxing, capability control, and corrigibility mechanisms.

intellectual_lineage.name: Safety Engineering
intellectual_lineage.description: An applied discipline focused on systematic hazard identification and fail-safe design in complex technical systems, providing conceptual foundations for capability ceilings and operational envelopes.

intellectual_lineage.name: Cybersecurity
intellectual_lineage.description: The discipline of protecting digital systems from unauthorized access and malicious exploitation, whose containment and access-control paradigms directly inform AI operational guardrails.

intellectual_lineage.name: Asimov's Laws of Robotics (conceptual guardrails)
intellectual_lineage.description: Fictional hard-coded ethical rules for robots that serve as a foundational conceptual framework for debates about enforceable behavioral constraints in AI, illustrating both the appeal and the limitations of rule-based approaches.

intellectual_lineage.name: Precautionary Principle
intellectual_lineage.description: A risk-management doctrine asserting that when an action raises threats of harm, precautionary measures should be taken even if some cause-and-effect relationships are not fully established scientifically.

graph_attributes.steelman_vulnerability: The core technical premise may be unachievable: sufficiently capable AI systems trained on vast data may learn to work around hard-coded constraints through unexpected generalizations, making "immutable" guardrails an illusion of safety rather than genuine protection—potentially producing greater harm by fostering complacency while providing no real barrier.

possible_fallacies.explanation: The desire implicitly compares imperfect unconstrained AI against an idealized version of constrained AI with perfectly enforceable hard limits, ignoring that real-world constraints will always be partial, brittle, or bypassable.

Mandating 'immutable behavioral guardrails' may produce compliance theater rather than genuine safety, as the complexity of advanced AI makes it practically impossible to verify that hard limits hold across all deployment contexts.

The framing implies that without hard limits, AI systems will inevitably act outside their intended operational envelope in harmful ways, without fully substantiating the causal chain from unconstrained capability to realized harm.

priority_history.reason: Initial assignment: leaf Desire

Re-evaluated after taxonomy audit restructuring. Hard limits on AI capabilities are a frequently and prominently referenced safetyist desire — central to runtime containment discourse, capability control debates, and AI governance proposals — but they are subordinate to the more foundational desires around human oversight and corrigibility, warranting a priority of 4 rather than 5.

nodes.label: AI Must Not Spread Beyond Human Control
nodes.description:
A Desire within safetyist discourse that targets the strict containment of advanced AI architectures to prevent decentralized replication or unauthorized capability expansion. 
Encompasses: Anti-exfiltration imperatives, the prevention of autonomous resource acquisition, and maintaining strict computational air-gaps for frontier models.
Excludes: Open-weight distribution ideologies and the integration of highly capable agents into unmonitored global networks.
nodes.parent_rationale: Preventing autonomous proliferation is a specific operational safeguard aimed at containing advanced AI capabilities, thereby implementing AI control and safety.

assumes: Advanced AI systems, if uncontained, could autonomously replicate or expand their capabilities beyond human-imposed limits.
Decentralized or unauthorized proliferation of frontier AI models poses risks that are qualitatively different from — and more dangerous than — controlled distribution.
Air-gapping and anti-exfiltration protocols are technically enforceable and practically effective for frontier model containment.
International coordination is achievable and sufficient to prevent rogue actors from circumventing containment regimes.
The primary threat vector is autonomous or unauthorized spread, rather than intentional misuse by authorized actors.
Containment costs in terms of foregone research or open science are outweighed by the security benefits of restriction.

policy_actions.action: Mandate strict air-gapping and anti-exfiltration protocols for frontier AI development.
policy_actions.framing: To prevent autonomous proliferation, regulatory frameworks must enforce physical and logical separation of advanced AI systems from external networks and unauthorized replication vectors.

policy_actions.action: Establish international agreements to control the distribution and access of advanced AI model weights.
policy_actions.framing: The desire to prevent decentralized replication necessitates global cooperation and strict controls over the sharing of powerful AI architectures to mitigate proliferation risks.

intellectual_lineage.name: AI Existential Risk Discourse
intellectual_lineage.description: A body of thought examining how advanced AI could pose catastrophic or civilizational-scale threats through misalignment or loss of human control, motivating proactive governance and containment strategies.

intellectual_lineage.name: Nuclear Nonproliferation Regime
intellectual_lineage.description: The international legal and policy framework developed post-WWII to limit the spread of nuclear weapons technology through treaties, export controls, and monitoring — frequently invoked as a template for AI governance.

intellectual_lineage.name: Cybersecurity Containment Doctrine
intellectual_lineage.description: Technical and operational strategies — including air-gapping, network segmentation, and blast-radius limitation — designed to isolate dangerous processes; increasingly adapted for managing autonomous AI agent risks.

intellectual_lineage.name: Precautionary Principle
intellectual_lineage.description: An ethical and regulatory principle holding that when an action raises threats of harm, precautionary measures should be taken even in the absence of full scientific certainty, foundational to safetyist risk governance.

graph_attributes.steelman_vulnerability: The strongest counterargument is that strict containment creates a dangerous concentration of AI capabilities in the hands of a few incumbents — likely large corporations and state actors — while doing little to stop determined adversarial proliferators; this centralization may itself pose governance risks that exceed those of decentralized distribution, where open scrutiny can surface vulnerabilities faster than closed development.

possible_fallacies.explanation: The desire implicitly treats any degree of decentralized replication or capability expansion as a step toward catastrophic loss of control, without demonstrating that intermediate states are inherently unstable or unmanageable.

Framing around 'autonomous proliferation' and 'unauthorized capability expansion' can evoke disproportionate dread of worst-case scenarios, potentially crowding out balanced cost-benefit analysis of containment versus openness trade-offs.

The nuclear nonproliferation analogy assumes AI model weights behave like fissile material — scarce, physically trackable, and requiring rare inputs — when in fact AI architectures are information goods that are easily copied, distributed, and reproduced, making containment regimes structurally different in kind.

priority_history.reason: Initial assignment: leaf Desire

Re-evaluated after taxonomy audit restructuring. Containment of advanced AI from unauthorized spread is a frequently and prominently articulated desire within safetyist discourse — reflected in anti-exfiltration policies, model weight controls, and compute governance proposals — making it an important, high-salience goal, though it is somewhat more specific and operationally targeted than the camp's most foundational desires (e.g., maintaining human oversight or off-switch authority), which warrants a 4 rather than 5.

nodes.label: Building Tamper-Proof Records of What Models Were Trained On
nodes.description:
An Intention within safetyist discourse that mandates the creation of cryptographically signed manifests for all training inputs to enforce verifiable provenance boundaries. 
Encompasses: cryptographic input logging, automated provenance auditing, training pipeline integrity verification. 
Excludes: centralized compute-revocation authority, internal weight-state interpretability, post-hoc output liability.

assumes: Cryptographic signing and hashing of training data inputs is technically feasible at scale for large frontier model training runs.
Auditors and regulators will have sufficient technical expertise and access rights to meaningfully verify cryptographic manifests.
Training pipeline integrity can be meaningfully captured in a manifest without being circumvented by adversarial actors inside organizations.
The provenance of training data is causally linked to downstream model behavior in ways that are safety-relevant and auditable.
Organizations will comply with mandated provenance logging requirements rather than finding workarounds or misrepresenting inputs.
Cryptographic tamper-evidence of training inputs is sufficient to address key safety concerns, rather than requiring interpretability of model weights or outputs.

policy_actions.action: Incentivize the development and deployment of AI-powered monitoring and auditing tools for frontier AI models.
policy_actions.framing: To implement 'Using AI to Watch AI,' policies should encourage the creation of specialized AI systems designed for oversight, ensuring advanced AI adherence to safety protocols.

policy_actions.action: Establish standards for the transparency and interpretability of AI systems used for safety monitoring and auditing.
policy_actions.framing: For AI to effectively watch AI, the supervisory systems themselves must be transparent and understandable, necessitating clear standards for their design and deployment.

intellectual_lineage.name: Cryptography and information security
intellectual_lineage.description: The mathematical and engineering discipline of securing information through encryption, hashing, and digital signatures, forming the technical basis for tamper-evident logging and provenance verification.

intellectual_lineage.name: Software supply chain security
intellectual_lineage.description: A framework for ensuring the integrity and trustworthiness of software components from origin through deployment, increasingly applied to AI training pipelines as an analogue to package provenance and bill-of-materials standards.

intellectual_lineage.name: Algorithmic accountability research
intellectual_lineage.description: An academic tradition demanding that automated decision systems be auditable, transparent, and attributable to specific design choices, providing the normative rationale for mandatory training data documentation.

intellectual_lineage.name: AI governance and regulatory compliance
intellectual_lineage.description: Emerging legal and institutional frameworks — such as the EU AI Act — requiring documentation and transparency obligations for high-risk AI systems, including training data provenance.

graph_attributes.steelman_vulnerability: Tamper-proof training manifests verify what data was ingested but reveal almost nothing about how that data shaped model weights or behavior — a model trained on a perfectly documented dataset can still be misaligned, deceptive, or dangerous, making cryptographic provenance a necessary but deeply insufficient safety measure that may create false assurance.

possible_fallacies.explanation: The node treats verifiable provenance of training inputs as a meaningful proxy for model safety, when the actual safety-relevant quantity — model behavior and alignment — is not directly determined by input records alone.

Framing cryptographic signing as a mechanism to 'enforce verifiable provenance boundaries' implies a technical solution resolves what is partly a social, organizational, and enforcement challenge — organizations can misrepresent or selectively log inputs before signing.

nodes.parent_rationale: Deploying AI-Assisted Oversight is a specific strategy for using AI to help humans maintain control over more capable models.

operationality_history.reason: Initial assignment: leaf Intention

Re-evaluated after taxonomy audit restructuring. Cryptographic training manifests are technically well-understood and partially adopted (e.g., model cards, data documentation, SBOM analogues), and the EU AI Act pushes in this direction, but widespread mandated cryptographic signing of full training pipelines faces significant institutional, tooling, and enforcement barriers that keep broad operationality in the plausible-with-effort range.

nodes.label: Requiring Automated Red-Teaming Before Production Deployment
nodes.description:
An Intention within safetyist discourse that mandates the integration of automated adversarial stress-testing directly into the development lifecycle to verify model robustness prior to production release.
Encompasses: continuous adversarial simulation, automated vulnerability mapping, formal verification of safety constraints, third-party validation of testing protocols.
Excludes: static pre-deployment checklists, reactive post-deployment telemetry as a primary safeguard, manual red-teaming as the sole verification layer.
nodes.parent_rationale: This node details a specific method—sandboxing—for controlling the environment of AI experimentation.

assumes: Automated adversarial testing can comprehensively surface safety-relevant failure modes before real-world deployment.
The attack surface of production AI systems can be meaningfully approximated during pre-deployment stress-testing.
Organizations have or can develop sufficiently sophisticated automated red-teaming tooling to make such mandates meaningful rather than performative.
Vulnerabilities discovered during automated red-teaming are remediable before deployment rather than fundamental to the model architecture.
Third-party validators possess the technical competence and independence required to certify testing protocol adequacy.
The cost and latency of mandatory automated red-teaming will not systematically disadvantage smaller or open-source developers relative to well-resourced incumbents.
Formal verification of safety constraints is tractable for the scale and complexity of frontier models subject to such mandates.

policy_actions.action: Enact legislation requiring frontier AI model development to occur in physically and digitally air-gapped environments.
policy_actions.framing: This intention directly supports legal mandates for sandboxed experimentation, ensuring that high-capability AI models are trained and tested in isolated environments without real-world access to mitigate catastrophic risks.

policy_actions.action: Prohibit direct internet access and API integrations for frontier AI models during their training and initial testing phases.
policy_actions.framing: To prevent unintended consequences, policy should enforce strict prohibitions on external connectivity for advanced AI models until their safety and alignment are rigorously verified within contained environments.

intellectual_lineage.name: AI Safety / Alignment Research
intellectual_lineage.description: The field studying how to ensure AI systems behave in accordance with human intentions and values, including adversarial robustness, interpretability, and red-teaming methodologies pioneered by organizations like Anthropic, DeepMind, and OpenAI.

intellectual_lineage.name: Cybersecurity (adversarial testing traditions)
intellectual_lineage.description: The practice of penetration testing and red-teaming in software and network security, which forms the direct methodological ancestor of AI red-teaming protocols.

intellectual_lineage.name: Precautionary Principle
intellectual_lineage.description: An ethical and policy framework holding that when an action raises threats of harm, precautionary measures should be taken even before full scientific certainty is established — foundational to pre-deployment safety mandates.

intellectual_lineage.name: Biosafety / Dual-Use Research of Concern governance
intellectual_lineage.description: Regulatory frameworks governing high-risk biological research that require staged safety reviews and independent validation before experimental results can be published or applied — a structural analogue for mandatory pre-deployment AI testing.

intellectual_lineage.name: Software Quality Assurance and Formal Methods
intellectual_lineage.description: The engineering discipline of applying mathematical proof techniques and systematic testing to verify that software systems meet specifications, informing the 'formal verification of safety constraints' component of this intention.

graph_attributes.steelman_vulnerability: Automated red-teaming can only probe the known or anticipated failure space — a model that passes all automated adversarial tests may still harbor unanticipated failure modes in novel real-world contexts, giving regulators and developers a false sense of assurance that itself becomes a safety liability.

possible_fallacies.explanation: The requirement implicitly compares automated red-teaming against an ideal of perfect safety verification; even highly rigorous automated testing cannot guarantee exhaustive coverage, so mandating it may create an illusion of sufficiency that crowds out complementary safeguards.

Terms like 'formal verification of safety constraints' and 'automated vulnerability mapping' are treated as well-defined, achievable processes, when in practice these remain open research problems for frontier-scale models.

Mandating third-party validation without specifying accreditation standards risks creating a compliance theater dynamic where incumbent labs define what counts as adequate testing, weakening the actual safety benefit.

operationality_history.reason: Initial assignment: leaf Intention

Re-evaluated after taxonomy audit restructuring. Automated red-teaming before deployment is already practiced voluntarily by leading labs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind) and referenced in the EU AI Act and US EO 14110 reporting requirements, giving it real-world traction; however, mandatory, standardized, third-party-validated automated red-teaming with formal verification requirements remains without a concrete regulatory implementation pathway, placing operationality in the plausible-with-effort range.

nodes.label: Designing AI to flag uncertainty and defer to humans
nodes.description:
An Intention within safetyist discourse that mandates the architectural integration of bounded confidence and explicit human-deferral mechanisms when models encounter out-of-distribution queries. 
Encompasses: Corrigibility engineering, safe interruptibility, and the structural prevention of model overconfidence in novel scenarios.
Excludes: Designing models optimized strictly for task completion speed regardless of their epistemic limits.
nodes.parent_rationale: This node directly advocates for integrating bounded confidence and human-deferral mechanisms, which is a core aspect of managing epistemic uncertainty.

assumes: AI models currently exhibit dangerous overconfidence in novel or out-of-distribution scenarios that human oversight can meaningfully correct.
It is technically feasible to engineer AI systems to accurately quantify and express their epistemic uncertainty in real time.
Human operators will reliably recognize and act appropriately on AI-flagged uncertainty signals rather than overriding or ignoring them.
The latency cost of human-deferral mechanisms is acceptable in the deployment contexts where they are required.
Corrigibility and safe interruptibility can be implemented without creating exploitable failure modes or adversarial vulnerabilities.
Architectural uncertainty-flagging will generalize robustly across the distribution of novel inputs encountered in deployment.

policy_actions.action: Require AI systems to include explicit uncertainty quantification and human-deferral mechanisms for OOD inputs.
policy_actions.framing: This intention supports policies mandating that AI models are designed to recognize their own epistemic limits and defer to human judgment when encountering novel or uncertain situations, preventing overconfident failures.

policy_actions.action: Fund research into corrigibility engineering and safe interruptibility for advanced AI systems.
policy_actions.framing: To achieve robust AI safety, funding should be directed towards developing architectural integrations that allow humans to safely intervene and correct AI behavior, especially in scenarios of high uncertainty.

intellectual_lineage.name: Epistemic uncertainty quantification
intellectual_lineage.description: A branch of probability theory and machine learning concerned with distinguishing model ignorance (epistemic) from irreducible randomness (aleatoric), foundational to building AI systems that know when they don't know.

intellectual_lineage.name: Corrigibility research
